solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Detectives from the continent reportedly outsourcing services?

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the phrase before it is judged by how it is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: detectives are private eyes, and someone from the continent of Asia is Asian; said together the two run into one word

explanation.surface: Foreign sleuths are said to be handling contracted-out work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private eyes Asian' spoken quickly gives the answer. The question mark marks the definition as loose: handing services to outside firms is what this policy amounts to.
explanation.definitionFit: Transferring state-run services to private firms is a form of contracting them out to external providers.

clue.text: Establish conditions for Spooner to do the job for free?

indicators.note: Spooner, the Oxford don famous for swapping the starts of words, signals that the initial sounds of a phrase are exchanged

parts.note: to work unpaid is to waive the pay, give up one's wages
the second word of that phrase, pay, takes the other swapped sound

explanation.surface: A volunteer offers to set things up at no charge, as Spooner might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waive the pay' with its opening W and P sounds exchanged becomes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To prepare the ground for something to happen is an idiom for creating the conditions it needs.

clue.text: Prominent members of French family falling into disrepute

indicators.note: the prominent members of a word are its leading letters, here the first three of the French word
in a down entry falling means those leading letters drop lower in the word

parts.note: the French word for family is famille

explanation.surface: The leading figures of a French dynasty slide into dishonour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prominent members of' picks FAM, the top of FAMILLE; 'falling' drops it below ILL, leaving ILL FAM E.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad reputation, as in a house of ill fame, is the state of being in disrepute.

clue.text: Being germ-free, passes freely round institute

indicators.note: round means the jumbled letters go around another piece
freely tells us the letters of passes may be arranged as we like

explanation.surface: Something passes freely around an institute while staying sterile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freely' turns PASSES into ASEPSS, and 'round' puts it around I to make ASEPS-I-S.
explanation.definitionFit: The medical term for the absence of infecting microorganisms, the condition of sterile surgery.

clue.text: What could make Bin Laden tick — what timeless, fundamentalist way of viewing things

indicators.note: could make says the letters that follow can be reworked into something new
timeless means the letter for time, T, is removed

parts.note: the second what, which loses its T

explanation.surface: Asks what drove Bin Laden: a starkly fundamentalist outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: BIN LADEN, TICK and WHA (what with 'timeless' removing T) together are shuffled by 'could make' into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeing everything as clear-cut good or evil, with no grey areas, is a hallmark of fundamentalist thinking.

clue.text: Who's allowed to participate in rearranged heat?

definitions.text: Who's allowed to participate in rearranged heat?

indicators.note: to participate in means one piece enters the middle of another
rearranged says the letters of heat are put in a new order

parts.note: allowed means let, as in permitted

explanation.surface: Asks who gets a place in a race that has been rescheduled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rearranged' shuffles heat to ATHE and 'to participate in' sets the permission inside. Read whole, the clue also describes the answer: a competitor entered in a qualifying race.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports competitor is the person permitted to run in a qualifying race of a track meeting.

clue.text: I get number 6 north of junction — alternatively, come up by tube?

indicators.note: in a down entry, north of means the earlier pieces sit above the next one

parts.note: VI is 6 in Roman numerals
a T-junction gives T for junction

indicators.note: in a down entry come up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: alternatively means or

explanation.surface: Someone is at junction 6 heading north, wondering whether to take the Underground instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The tube of the definition is a test tube, not the London Underground the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Laboratory processes done in glassware, such as test-tube fertilisation, are described with this Latin phrase meaning 'in glass'.

clue.text: Pet menu chez Hubbard not in English?

parts.note: non is the French for not, with chez in the clue setting a French tone

explanation.surface: Asks whether Mother Hubbard's dog menu lacked any English dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Old Mother Hubbard went to her cupboard for her dog's bone and found it bare, so the dog had nothing to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: The dog's dinner in the rhyme was nothing at all, so its menu consisted of zero items.

clue.text: Slim 12's transformed after losing weight

indicators.note: transformed means the remaining letters change into a new arrangement
after losing means a piece is first taken away

parts.note: the number 12 written out with the possessive gives twelves

explanation.surface: A dieter whose number has been changed by shedding pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' looks like a cross-reference to 12-across but is just the number. Removing W from TWELVES leaves TELVES, which 'transformed' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a slender, gracefully thin figure, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Crosby covers have reinterpreted what Fats was up to?

indicators.note: covers means one piece wraps around another

parts.note: Bing Crosby, the American crooner

indicators.note: reinterpreted means the letters of have are read in a new order

explanation.surface: Bing Crosby recorded cover versions, reinterpreting what Fats Waller had played.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reinterpreted' turns HAVE into EHAV, which BING covers. Fats Waller wrote 'Ain't Misbehavin'', so by his own song's double negative he was being good.
explanation.definitionFit: Waller's song title denies misconduct, and a double negative like that means acting properly.

clue.text: Frank — sex-change dad?

parts.note: trans is the short term for transgender, someone who has changed gender
a dad is a parent

explanation.surface: Asks whether Frank is a father who has changed sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' poses as a man's name; it is the definition, meaning candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Being open and honest, with nothing concealed, is to be easily seen through, so both mean candid.

clue.text: Tree missed badly here?

indicators.note: badly means the letters of tree missed are messed up into a new order

explanation.surface: Wonders whether this is a place where trees are sorely lacking.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also a description: in dry scrubland trees are badly missed.
explanation.definitionFit: Arid land with sparse vegetation lies between true desert and grassland, so trees are rare there.

clue.text: Find love back in tents

indicators.note: back means the words are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to find, as in to spot, is to see
love as a term of endearment is pet

explanation.surface: Someone discovers romance again while camping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns both words round together, so the second word ends up first.
explanation.definitionFit: Conical dwellings of hide or canvas used by Native Americans of the Plains are a kind of tent.

clue.text: This could make the pride of Wales collapse

parts.words: This could make the pride of Wales
parts.note: the leek is the national emblem and pride of Wales; turning the first word of the answer over spells it, so the answer read as an instruction yields the emblem

explanation.surface: Something that might bring down Wales's proudest possession.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read as wordplay, the answer says to turn K-E-E-L over, which makes the Welsh emblem L-E-E-K.
explanation.definitionFit: To topple or faint suddenly, like a capsizing boat, is an idiom for collapsing.

clue.text: Leave west end of city at 10 in transit, perhaps

indicators.note: in means the pieces go inside another

parts.note: the Ford Transit is a common British van, so a Transit is an example of a van

indicators.note: in an across entry the west end is the first letter

parts.note: 10 written as figures one and zero gives the letters I and O

explanation.surface: Someone leaves the West End of a city at ten, travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West end' tempts toward London's West End; it means the first letter of city. Ford Transit is a long-selling British van, so a van is a 'transit, perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Leave in the sense of time off work is a holiday, the American word for it.

clue.text: Something like Funky Gibbon's in the charts? Crazy!

parts.note: a gibbon is an ape, so something like it with the possessive gives ape's
a record in the charts is a hit

explanation.surface: Wonders whether 'Funky Gibbon' being in the charts was madness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funky Gibbon' was a 1975 UK chart novelty song by the comedy group The Goodies.
explanation.definitionFit: A vulgar slang word for wild or frenzied, describing someone going berserk.

clue.text: Where to find meat and two veg at lunchtime consumes you and I — it's essential

indicators.note: consumes means one piece swallows another inside it

parts.words: Where to find meat and two veg at lunchtime
parts.note: a BLT sandwich holds bacon, lettuce and tomato, meat and two veg, so these are found in a BLT
U is text-speak for you

explanation.surface: A lunchtime meal of meat and two veg eats us both up: it's vital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meat and two veg' suggests a traditional British dinner; here it is a BLT (bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwich).
explanation.definitionFit: Something integral, built into a thing's basic nature, is fundamental to it.

clue.text: Job that is for one regularly given the sack

parts.note: a job is a post

explanation.surface: A job that means someone keeps getting fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given the sack' seems to mean dismissed; it is the postbag handed out every day. Postie is British slang for the mail carrier.
explanation.definitionFit: The mail carrier is handed a bag of letters each day, so is literally given the sack daily.

clue.text: Standard place falling short for social climber

parts.note: par is the standard or norm

indicators.note: falling short means the word stops one letter before its end

parts.note: a venue is a place

explanation.surface: A status-seeker whose usual spot comes up lacking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falling short' removes the last E from VENUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone newly risen in wealth or status but not accepted by those above is an upstart.

clue.text: Boys from the south pinching American's bum is a disgrace

indicators.note: pinching means one piece holds another between its letters
in a down entry, from the south means the word is read upward

parts.note: lads are boys
can is American slang for the buttocks

explanation.surface: Southern lads groping an American's backside is shameful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the south' reads the boys upward as SDAL in this down entry; 'bum' is US slang here, not British.
explanation.definitionFit: An event causing public outrage is a shameful affair, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Joint musical effort

parts.note: the elbow is a joint of the arm
Grease is a well-known stage and film musical

explanation.surface: A collaborative musical undertaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' reads as shared; it is a body joint.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard physical work, especially vigorous scrubbing, is the idiom's meaning.

clue.text: Game over for fashion

indicators.note: over means the word is turned upside down, read upward in this down entry

parts.note: brag is a card game, an ancestor of poker

explanation.surface: Playtime's over; time for style.
explanation.definitionFit: A distinctive style of dress, as in clerical attire, is a manner or fashion of clothing.

clue.text: One from subcontinent made his mark clumsily before independence

indicators.note: before places the jumbled piece ahead of the next
clumsily means the letters of his mark are put together awkwardly in a new order

parts.note: I is a standard abbreviation for independence or independent

explanation.surface: A man from India awkwardly signed his name before independence in 1947.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clumsily' rearranges HIS MARK into KASHMIR; 'before' puts it ahead of I.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Himalayan region in the north of the Indian subcontinent.

clue.text: Media boss passes round flowers

parts.note: an editor, ED, runs a newspaper or magazine
passes, as in passes away, means dies

explanation.surface: A media executive hands round bouquets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flowers' are blooms in the surface; here they are things that flow, and 'round' joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Whirling currents of water or air circle around, so they are circular flows.

clue.text: Take bull by the horns? Grasp it in broken teeth, I bet!

indicators.note: grasp means the shuffled letters grip something
in means a piece is placed inside the shuffled letters
broken means the letters of teeth and I bet are smashed into a new order

parts.note: it refers back to the bull of the definition

explanation.surface: Seize the beast in your broken teeth — I dare you!
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' points back to the animal in the definition; 'broken' rearranges the fodder around it, making the clue nearly self-describing.
explanation.definitionFit: Both idioms mean confronting a hard or unpleasant situation bravely rather than avoiding it.
